analysis.one_liner: Bars courts from sealing case records and settlements that hide public health and safety dangers.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved this court-secrecy bill with bipartisan support in August 2008, but the full Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies facing lawsuits over dangerous products or practices routinely ask courts to seal the evidence and ban the other side from ever talking about the settlement. This bill would require a judge to find that an order doesn't hide information relevant to public health or safety before approving it, would let parties report problems to government regulators even under a secrecy deal, and would stop courts from enforcing gag clauses that keep settlement facts quiet. Judges could still seal records for a strong, specific reason like personal privacy.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, injured people, and regulators. When a company settles a lawsuit over a defective product or a harmful drug, the evidence usually disappears behind a court's protective order, and the next customers never hear about it. The bill would shift the default: courts could only hide health and safety information after weighing the public's interest in knowing, and no settlement could stop a party from reporting the problem to the federal or state agency that regulates it.

how_it_helps.text: Before a court could enter a protective order, approve a settlement that restricts disclosure, or seal court records, it would have to find that the order would not restrict information relevant to protecting public health or safety, or that a specific and substantial confidentiality interest outweighs the public's interest in learning about potential hazards, and that the order is no broader than necessary.
No party could demand, as a condition of turning over evidence, that the other side agree to a secrecy order that violates the act.

Courts could not approve or enforce any agreement that stops a party from disclosing relevant information to a federal or state agency with authority to regulate the activity in question, so regulators would keep learning about hazards even after a case settles.

Courts could not enforce settlement clauses barring a party from saying a settlement happened, describing its terms (other than the dollar amount), or discussing case evidence involving public health or safety, unless the court finds confidentiality outweighs the public interest in disclosure.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate defendants in product-liability, drug, and consumer-safety litigation, who now often resolve cases under protective orders and confidentiality agreements that keep the underlying evidence and safety problems out of public view. The bill would force that evidence into the open whenever it bears on health or safety, which these firms argue could discourage settlements and expose trade secrets and competitively sensitive material.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that broad disclosure rules could sweep in legitimate secrets: the bill answers part of this by creating a rebuttable presumption that protecting a person's identifiable financial or health information outweighs disclosure, and by explicitly exempting classified information, but companies contend trade secrets and sensitive business records would still be harder to protect.

Defendants and some litigators argue that the prospect of public disclosure makes settlement harder and costlier to reach, which can delay compensation for injured plaintiffs, and that dictating protective-order standards by statute intrudes on rules that courts themselves set.
The bill applies only prospectively, to orders and agreements entered 30 days after enactment, so it would not unseal existing settlements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is real and targeted: the bill keeps the core protections for genuinely private matters (personal financial and health information, classified material) while removing courts' routine blessing of secrecy that hides safety hazards. The cost falls on defendants who lose a litigation-management tool, and the burden of proving secrecy is justified shifts to whoever wants it. On balance the trade favors disclosure, which is why it drew bipartisan support; the honest caveat is that any blanket rule can catch close cases, and the bill relies on judges to draw the line case by case.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it with an amendment and put it on the Senate's calendar of business in August 2008, but the chamber never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Herb Kohl introduced the bill on December 11, 2007, with Sens. Patrick Leahy and Lindsey Graham, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in March 2008 and formally reported it on August 1, 2008, with a written report.
The reported version added a rebuttable presumption protecting individuals' personal financial and health information and a carve-out for classified information.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 935) on August 1, 2008, and no further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate defendants keep the ability to settle safety cases under sealed, gagged agreements; the public never got the disclosure rules. The bill was reintroduced in later Congresses and never became law.

for.name: Herb Kohl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sunshine in Litigation Act and led it through the Senate.

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably out of the Judiciary Committee with an amendment and a written report on August 1, 2008.

for.name: Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Committee on the Judiciary
for.what_they_did: Held a markup in March 2008 and voted to report the bill favorably with an amendment.

against.name: Senate leadership of the 110th Congress
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and floor schedulers
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the legislative calendar in August 2008; it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican original cosponsor (Sen. Graham) alongside Democrats Kohl and Leahy, two cosponsors split 1 D and 1 R, and cleared committee favorably with no recorded opposition, so the failure to reach a vote was not a partisan vote on the merits.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants in product-liability and drug litigation (manufacturers, drug makers, insurers)
industries.note: These companies routinely obtain protective orders and confidentiality clauses that keep litigation evidence about product and drug hazards sealed. The bill would let courts approve such secrecy only after weighing the public's interest in knowing about health and safety dangers, and would guarantee that settlement parties can still report problems to regulators.

industries.industry: Court reporting, legal transparency, and public-interest journalism
industries.note: More unsealed records and enforceable limits on gag clauses mean reporters and public-interest groups can see and report on hazards disclosed in court cases. Ordinary consumers are the downstream beneficiaries of that information.
